I did not intend to allude to any personal matter, but it was brought on'by the Minister of Customs himself. I want to say, so far as that gentleman is concerned, that he is looking after the biscuit industry of this country, if he is not looking after the woollen industry.
So far as the preferential tariff is concerned, I hold that this government are doing a great injustice to the towns of Canada. In the town of Peterborough, as in other towns, we have done everything we could, in the way of exemption from taxes and otherwise, to have manufactories located there. The object was to build up our town. And after the people of this country, both in Ontario and Quebec, have given all the encouragement they could, in exemption from taxation, in buildings and lands in some cases, for the promotion of manufacturing, this government comes forward and takes it all away. In my place in this House, I want to denounce in the strongest terms the preferential tariff of this government.
We had the minister without portfolio from Quebec (Mr. Dobell), saying the other
day that the people of Quebec were perfectly satisfied with the tariff. I understood him to say that the shoe industry of Quebec was perfectly satisfied with it. Did he say that ?
No, I did not.

Well, I will read what the hon. gentleman did say. I want to show his position, because I understand that in Quebec there is an industry suffering greatly under this tariff, and I want to get him right. He said :
I claim tor the present government of Canada that they have passed a resolution by which the products of Great Britain are admitted in the rate of their tariff at 12S per cent, and next year at 25 per cent reduction. This we have done, not asking any compensation. There is a class of our fellow-citizens who ask that all such concessions should be made for a quid pro quo. The Canadian government has ignored such sentiments. We have done it because we owe a debt of gratitude to Great Britain. We have done it because it is no intention of ours to disturb in any way the system of free trade which has done so much for England.
I understand that the hon. gentleman is a free trader. We want to know where he stands.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to put myself right so far as the preferential tariff Is concerned. I do not speak for my leader in this House; I am quite satisfied with his resolution; but in what I say, I am speaking for myself, and I condemn in the strongest terms any preference to any other country. That is my position to-day.

May I say a word in explanation ? What the hon. gentleman quoted a few moments ago was what Sir Wilfrid Laurier stated on his arrival in Liverpool. I gave it as a quotation, and I was very proud of it as coming from the lips of a Canadian.
And you agreed with it ?
Entirely.

That is the same thing. Now. I want to say to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the premier of this country that 1 consider that these gentlemen have done a great injustice to this country. In 1S70 and 1877 I was in the manufacturing business. We all remember the deputations which came here to interview the government at that time; we know how those deputations were received; and I want to say that the deputations of manufacturers who come here to-day to wait on this government are received in exactly the same way. It has been said in this House that we do-not want any tinkering with the tariff; hut these gentlemen, ever since they came

into office, have been tinkering with the tariff. They first gave a preference of 12i per cent, then they altered it to 25 per cent, and afterwards they altered it to one-third. What is that but tinkering with the tariff ? I want to say that no man is warranted in going into manufacturing in this country to-day under this tariff. I would not invest one dollar in manufacturing in this country, with such a preference against me. If we owe England anything, let us pay it, no matter what it is-whether it is one million or two million dollars. But I say it is not fair to this country that the government should give this preference, not to England-we are not giving it to England-but to the manufacturers of Yorkshire. I say it is a matter of vested rights in this country; but it seems that we have no vested rights in this country which this government is not willing to legislate away.
Mr. Speaker, I hold in my hand a letter, part of which I intend to read to the House. I understand that the Prime Minister has received a copy of it. I mav say that it comes from the manufacturers' of this country as a whole, and not from any individual manufacturer. It is as follows :

Fielding,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-I beg to inclose herewith a paragraph taken from last week's Journal of Fabrics, showing the imports of woollen and worsted fabrics as compared with last year. You will notice a startling increase for the month of January, nearly 40 per cent, in woollen fabrics, and over 35 per cent in worsted fabrics. You will note also that there is a falling off in all other textile exports from Great Britain to Canada, except carpets, which is slightly increased, about 10 per cent.
When we interviewed you in Ottawa we told you that the 331 preferential rate had not fully gotten into operation, and that we should feel it when the spring imports were received. Our worst fears are more than realized. Our future looks desperate. Surely there is some way in which you can afford relief. There were over fifty employees discharged at the Auburn mills Peterboro', last week. Fifty more will be laid off this week, as the orders are being completed and no new orders coming in. During the past month we have discharged over 200 employees at Hespeler alone. Lomas's mill at Almonte, has completely closed down, and other mills are running on short time. The repeat orders for spung are of such small character, and coming in so slowly that it looks as though there would not be in six months from now 25 per cent of the woollen machinery in operation that there was in July of last year. I cannot think that you will allow that condition of affairs to continue. It is a case of life and death with us and matters should not be allowed to drift along until next year. Our help will be scattered I am informed by Mr. Brodie that forty-seven men left Hespeler last week for the United States. They left their families behind until they obtained work, when they propose to send for them. Our machinery will be lying idle and getting out of condition. Fixed charges will be running on, and there will be a very

ruinous loss of capital before the end of this year. Our general manager informs us that owing to the state of his orders he will be obliged to discharge over 200 more persons by the 10th April, which will leave only 400 at the mill, where we employed up to quite recently 800. I fear you do not. realize the serious condition of the woollen industry and the danger it is in of being completely extinguished.
Woollen machinery is only fit for making woollen goods, and buildings are erected especially for the convenience of manufacturing woollens. It is all very well for people who have no practical knowledge of these things to say with a light heart-as many members of parliament do in their speeches-* why not turn your attention to something else?' Well, when everything one has got is invested in an enterprise, what can he turn his attention to? It requires capital and experience to embark in any manufacturing enterprise. Our capital is invested in the woollen industry, and our experience is in the manufacturing of woollen goods. I venture to say that you do realize that the woollen industry is the only one that has been hit, and hit hard, and I may say, without the slightest exaggeration, is on the brink of ruin by the operation of the preferential tariff.
We do not object to the preference to Great Britain, we are prepared to support it, but the tariff should be so arranged that we should be put on an equality with the Lancashire manufacturers.
I can assure you that the situation is really serious, and the financial institutions who are supporting the various large woollen industries -what I mean by supporting Is discounting their paper and making them advances-are becoming seriously alarmed. If they withdraw their confidence and refuse to continue to make advances, the mills will have to close down, and that is just what is in sight, I fear.
It looks to us, and to a great many of the members of the House, that the woollen industry has been singled out for the severest competition, not only by reason of the peculiar advantage of British manufacturers of woollens, but by reason of the extent to which German goods are smuggled into Canada through Great Britain under pretense of partial manufacture in England. You will note that the several departments of the textile trade are relatively untouched by the preferential tariff. The silk trade, the linen trade, the jute trade, and the cotton trade all appear to be exempt from the severe competition suffered by the woollen mills.
I greatly regret to say that many members of the House I have spoken with do not vote as they talk, as I have been assured by many of them, including some members of the cabinet, that they were protectionists, and that we ought to have some relief; but they vote the other way when relief is asked for. I hate to put it in that way, but it is a true statement of the case.
In making this appeal I do so in the hope that the facts already before you, and the additional information contained therein will be fully and fairly considered by the government and that something will be done for us this session.
I have nothing more to say, Mr. Speaker, on this question except to express again the hope that the government will see its way to afford some relief to this very important industry.

Mr. Speaker, as a new member in this House, I deemed it more fitting that I should, during this, my first session, sit very quietly in the House and take in all that was happening around me. And therefore, on this occasion, I shall not take up the time of hon. members except for a very few moments.
Indeed I should not have risen were it not for certain arguments presented by some hon. gentlemen opposite on the question under discussion, on which I considered it necessary that, on account of the position I occupy, I should say a few words. The position is taken by these hon. gentlemen to whom I have referred, that the protection of the manufacturing industries of this country necessarily implies the prosperity of the labouring classes-that to have, for instance, the wheels of the woollen factories constantly revolving is always an evidence of the prosperity of the industrial classes. That proposition was started very strongly by the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean), the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock), the hon member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule), and the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Kendry). These hon. gentlemen all strove hard 'to impress this House and country with the idea that they are supporters of a high protective tariff, not merely on account of the manufacturers themselves, but more especially on account of the labouring men. That, Mr. Speaker, is the same old argument that was set up against the principles of Cobden and Bright. The argument set up in England, when the repeal of the principle of protection was brought about in that country, was the same that these hon. gentlemen have advanced, and as a representative, interested more particularly in the industrial classes from an organized standpoint, I wish to state that I do not believe at all in the principle which (these hon. gentlemen have enunciated.
With reference to the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean), I desire to say that I have taken a very great interest in that hon. gentleman. I have sat very quietly in this House, being anxious to learn, and to make haste slowly and see my way ahead, and have been very much interested, particularly in the hon. gentleman from East York. I was interested more particularly in what he said on the question before the House, and I will tell you why ? I thought that the position which he then took is very different to the strong and persistent one which he has hitherto taken. The hon. gentleman, previous to this debate, constantly advocated the claims of the people, as opposed to corporations and trusts, and took every occasion to bring to our attention the importance of guarding the interests of the people against these institutions, and I had
come to the conclusion that the position which the hon. gentleman took, so far as it could be made practicable, was deserving of my support. But what do we find in this debate ? I find that he is just taking the opposite course, and is doing his best to apply the principles of protection in favour of those very corporations and trusts, whose existence he had hitherto considered a menace.
I am working on behalf of the manufacturers and the Canadian workingmen.

I will prove before I get through that the hon. gentleman never mentioned the producers at all, but that the whole of his plea was for the manufacturers. On the one hand, he comes repeatedly before this House, advocating the interests of the people, in the shape of government ownership and control of industries. On the other hand, he comes on the floor of this House and asks the people of this coutnry to tax themselves in favour of that same class.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon
Oh, oh.
I wish to put the hon. gentleman right, and I hope he will allow me to do so.
Oh, oh.
The hon. gentleman does not want to be put right.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) described himself as an out-and-out protectionist.
Hear, hear-for Canadian labour.

The hon. gentleman never mentioned labour. He said he was a strong believer in government interference and in the authority of government. I believe-and I am glad to say it- that I also believe in the control of government. I believe that the political tendency of our time is to place greater authority in .the hands of the government and to make greater demands upon the government. But I take a different view of that question from that taken by the hon. member for East York. I believe in government interference for the weak against the strong, for the poor against the rich, for the masses against the few. And when the hon. gentleman advocates so persistently the principle of protection for the manufacturers, in my opinion it is not possible for him to render the best service to the workers of this country. There can be nothing in common between the call for high protection to the manufacturers end the demand for benefit for industrial classes.

The two principles are altogether opposite. The man who works for wages in the factory does not sell the products of the factory. If the competition is lessened in favour of the owners of the factory, and they are thus enabled to raise prices, how can the industrial classes be benefited ? The article produced by the labourer must be bought by the labourer as well as by others, and, if the price of the article is raised and the price of labour is not raised, by what course of reasoning is it to be shown that he is benefited ?
The hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) took the same position as the hon. member for East York, and the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) put up a strong plea in favour of the same position as that taken by the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Kendry)-in fact, both those gentlemen read the self same letters. All these hon. members put in a strong plea in favour of the industrial classes of this country, and have tried to show that if no greater protection is given to the manufacturers, the labouring men will have to move to the other side of the line. As I say, that is the old argument. But I do not at all believe that, when hon. gentlemen come to this House and seek special favour in the way of protecting their industries, the position of the industrial labourer is present to their minds at all. It is not with them a question how much the labourer should get; it is a question how large the profit of their particular industry should be. The whole history of the agitation of capital for the benefits of protection is a history of benefit to the capitalists themselves, without any reference to the condition of the labourer. Let 11s look for a few moments at the history of the case and consider some of the countries that are most highly protected. And here again, I wish to make some reference to the hon. member for East York, because he spoke on this line. Take the case of the United States. There you have an ideal country for the working of a protection system. If ever the principle of high protection could work out beneficially to a people, it would work out in favour of the people of the United States. You have there a country containing withiu its borders the greatest variety of natural wealth in the world-a country that produces everything necessary for the sustenance of life. That is a country where, if anywhere, they could afford to build a wall around their industries. And what is the condition of labour in the United States ? Has the protective principle, which has so greatly benefited certain capitalists, benefited correspondingly the producers and industrial labourers ? Mr. Speaker, the condition of the labour market in the United States in the most aggravated of any country in the world. It is beyond dispute that there are more strikes, more disturbances, greater difficulties in the way Mr. SMITH (Vancouver).
of industrial labour demanding a fair share of the product, there is more trouble and labour agitation in the United States, that highly protected country, than in any other country in the world. There is a greater combination of capital on the part of the workingmen, there is a stronger and more powerful organization of trades unionism than elsewhere, and there is constant agitation amongst the industrial labourers of that country to secure something like a reasonable share of the produce of their labour. In the United States they have an ideal condition for protection ; in the United States they have strikes, they have bloodshed, they have constant trouble and agitation, they have the militia sent to put down men, and women, and sometimes, even the children, as against the honest agitator who goes out to claim his rights. Can it be said that protection has benefited the American labourer or that he gets a greater share of the produce of his industry on account of protection ? Not at all. Now, let ns take the converse of all this-let us take the case of England. There you have a free trade country. Now, I am not advocating free trade for this country. I came from England a few years ago. I am glad to say that while I was there, I always found myself on the side of the reform movement of that country. However, I have observed conditions sufficiently to discover that it is not possible to carry out that free trade principle in this new and undeveloped country. I think that the government has the right ideal-a tariff for revenue. There is in that a tremendous force of protection. What is the condition of the labouring man in England ? A great deal has been said by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) about the labourer in England-and I am going to deal with that subject a little later on. The labouring men in England have greater numbers in their organizations and have greater benefits by legislation than they have in the United States. The legislation in favour of the industrial classes in England has some permanency. The factories in England today are better under the supervision of the government than are the American factories. And the factory operatives to-day have a better standard of wages-considerably better-than they have had for many years. Now, the hon. member for Centre Toronto mentioned the other evening, that one of the difficulties of the manufacturers in this country was the dearness of the fuel they had to import from the eastern states, as compared with the cheapness of the fuel necessary for the operation of the factories in England. Nott a single argument that has been put before this House affords a stronger condemnation of the principle of protection than that. I wish to ask the hon. member for Centre Toronto how it is that they have to pay more for the fuel than the manufacturers in England have to pay ? Is it difference in the labour ? Does the
man who digs the coal in England get less than the man who digs the coal in Pennsylvania ? As a matter of fact, the coal miner in England to-day has a larger wage than the coal miner in Pennsyslvania. Then the dearness of the article is not because the labourer has benefited, but because of the intermediate agencies that handle this product.

Will the hon. gentleman allow me to interrupt him ? How many months in the year do they require to heat their factories in England, and how many months in a year do they require to heat their factories in Canada ? Quantity as well as price has got to be taken into consideration.

like to have an answer. Are these signs of depression or of prosperity ? There are evidences to show that since the preferential tariff came into force the energies of this company have been stimulated ; as a matter of fact they have equipped their factory thoroughly with up-to-date machinery-that has all been done, mind you, since 1897. The machinery itself was said to have cost $50,000, and it is an undoubted fact that during these last few years they have turned out a much higher and finer class of goods than at any time in their history.
Let me mention that in British Columbia five or six years ago the people would not go into the stores and purchase Canadian manufactures, but to-day there is a growing disposition in favour of them, people are going into the stores and demanding Canadian woollens. I say there is a stronger demand for Canadian manufactured articles than ever before, showing that the articles are of higher value. I state that these milils have doubled their output, they are paying fair wages to their employees and they have made an average dividend of at least 0 per cent. Now these are very strong statements made on the floor of this House and hon. gentlemen must be in a position to answer them one way or another. If they are true, then where is the argument about the ruination of their property and of their business ? If they are not true, then we are driven to the conclusion that the hon. gentleman is prepared: to take a position that is not correct. I am credibly informed that this company did not pay any dividend at all in 1895-6 before the preferential tariff, but they were closed down entirely for intervals of weeks at a time. Ke-member, Mr. Speaker, at that particular time there was a Dominion election going on, and the hon. member for Peterborough was running in that election, and I want you to know that the mills were closed down at that particular time. And when protection is sought for by these hon. gentlemen the mills are very likely to be closed down again. But this is an old trick, we are used to that. Any one who knows anything at all about the history of labour is well aware that this is a trick often resorted to. Now, at that time the hon. member for Peterborough, speaking on a platform, said this :
If Sir Wilfrid Laurler was returned to power his factories at Peterborough that were closed at that time would never be opened again.
Now I want the hon. members of this House to remember what I have already stated. They have made large profits, they have employed more men, they have doubled their output, they have enhanced the value of their productions since the preferential tariff came into operation ; and yet at that very time the hon. gentleman stated that if the Liberal government came into power it would ruin his business.

Now, Sir, I did more than that. When I heard the statement read about the discharge of these men, I wanted to know if the hon. gentleman was saying exactly what was true, and I put myself to the trouble of having some very rapid correspondence with responsible men in Peterborough, and I am prepared to read the answers of those men in this House. I was anxious to know if the workingmen of this country were going to be driven out of employment, as the hon. gentleman had stated; I was very anxious about that question, because I was desirous of preventing a calamity of that kind. But I wanted to know what the facts were before I did anything. Now, this is the answer I received to questions as to the men being discharged and as to the possibilities of the mill being closed down : Ralph Smith, House of Commons.
Auburn woollen mills have been continually running night and day during these last four years

Now, these are the mills belonging to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kendry), who has just taken his seat.
-they have employed twice as many hands and have over twice as large a pay-roll as before, and turn out more than twice as much goods and of better quality than they did before.
This is a telegram that I am prepared to put on the records of this House, and when I am done reading it, I shall give the name of the sender.
They have improved their machinery out of their earnings at least $50,000, and have for three years been too busy to partly close down to accurately take stock, and as this is the period

I would like to remark that this is an explanation of very many things that have been said by hon. gentlemen opposite.
-as this is the period that they change from summer to winter goods, they now take stock and are extensively repairing their machinery and have laid off a very few hands temporarily for that purpose, as stock cannot be taken and machinery repaired with the mill running full capacity. They regularly pay good dividends to shareholders for five years, and are making money. Close and private corporation.
The name of this gentleman is to the telegram, and the tqjegram is sent by R. F. McGregor, chairman of the Associated Labourmen of the city of Peterborough. Now, Mr. Speaker, my experience with the strong plea in favour of protection has always been this : That the men who seek for special favours in the way of protection are always the men that object to protection when it comes down to the interests of the labouring classes.

Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Smith) excuse me for a minute. Before he drops that subject, would he tell us has he any information from the
Hespeler mills?
I have not; I have not had time to look into it.
Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Smith) attack any statement I made in connection with the woollen mills V What I stated referred to fifty mills in this country and not to one.

Special mention has been made of the mills at Peterborough. The hon. gentleman from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) read a most serious letter setting out that these mills had actually discharged their men and would he likely ito shut down, and the proprietor of these mills himself read that same letter on the floor of this House to-day. What I am doing is to prove to this House that there is no importance to be attached to that statement, as this telegram sets out.
I would like the hon. gentleman to read the telegram.
He has read it.

1 think the demand made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ivendry) is fair, and I will read it again:
Auburn woollen mills have been continually running night and day during this last tour years, have employed twice as many hands, and have over twice as large pay-roll as before, and turn out more than twice as much goods, and of better quality. They have Improved their machinery out of their earnings at least $50,000, and have for three years been too busy to partly close down to accurately take stock. As this is the period they change from summer to winter goods, they now take stock, and are extensively repairing their machinery, and have laid off very few hands temporarily for that purpose, as stock cannot be taken and machinery repaired with mill running at full capacity. Have regularly paid good dividends to shareholders for five years and are making money.

Will the hon. gentleman allow me. If the hon. gentleman will allow me to explain, I will explain exactly the position. Mr. Speaker, so far as that telegram is concerned, the whole statement is incorrect. We are to-day not doing any repairs at all, and we are closed on account of having no orders in the mill. Who- ; ever gave that information to Mr. Me-Gregor, the whole thing is incorrect.
What about the dividends ?

I have no disposition to dispute the word of an hon. member of this House. That is not my practice. But what I say is this : That I consider the authority of a disinterested man in Peterborough is of as much importance and far more likely to be correct than the statement of an hon. member of this House
Order.
Especially that of an hon. gentleman who has a direct interest in making a statement like this.
Order.
Mr. Speaker, I may say that I am one of the proprietors of that establishment, and surely I ought to know the position better than any outsider.
Hear, hear.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to take the full responsibility of what is stated in that telegram. I will be perfectly fair with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kendry). I am prepared to meet him under any proper conditions and to discuss this question with him, and if it is demonstrated by the hon. gentleman that this is incorrect, then of course, that view of the case can be presented.
He does not say it is incorrect.
Mr. Speaker, it is almost six o'clock, and I think I should be allowed to finish my remarks.
Go on.

No ; I want to speak for another five minutes, and then I shall finish. I wish to refer now to my hon. and genial friend the member for Victoria, and I want to do so because I want to mention a matter which illustrates the importance of the principle under discussion.
There are so many constituencies named Victoria, that I wish to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Smith) which, he refers to.
The genial one.
Which is that ?
You.

The senior member for Victoria, B.C. A few days ago we were discussing in this House the necessity of placing an import duty on lumber, and that is a question which very materially affects my interests as the representative of Vancouver Island. I may say, Sir, that I had telegrams from important bodies at that particular time asking me to support this resolution, but I disagreed with the resolution entirely. What I want to get at is this : In discussing that resolution the senior member for Victoria, B.C. (Hon. Mr. Prior) stated that the reason why the lumbermen of British Columbia at the present time had to employ Chinese and Japanese labour was because they were not able to compete with the American lumber manufacturers. This, Sir, is a matter which hears directly upon this discussion. I have been contending that the high protective tariff did not protect the labourer, but protected the manufacturer. The statement of the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Hon. Mr. Prior) was a very bold statement to make on the floor of this House.

speechtext: I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Smith) is referring to a past debate.

I am sure that the hon. gentleman from Victoria will not take any umbrage at what I am stating now. I will illustrate the point under discussion if I get time. That was a bold statement for the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Prior) to make, because the Chinese and Japanese were employed before the tariff was taken off by the Conservatives, and I want to ask my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Prior) can he give the House a guarantee that if the government impose a duty upon lumber coming into British Columbia corresponding with the duty on Canadian lumber : That Chinese and Japanese labour will be dispensed with. If the labourmen are protected by this protective tariff then we ought to be able to have a positive guarantee that that will be brought about. I want to tell my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Prior) that if he can give me that guarantee on the floor of this House then I will abandon my principles for once and support protection.
Hear, hear.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman an easier question than that still. I ask him: Suppose that this duty is imposed, can we have any guarantee that the white labourers of British Columbia would receive any more wages than they do now V That is the great question. Does protection protect the industrial classes ? Decidedly not. You put .?2 per thousand upon lumber coming into British Columbia ; you advance the price of lumber ;' you lessen the competition, but. Mr. Speaker, they have all the Chinese and Japanese they want in the labour market of that country to manufacture that lumber. I want to know if the lumbermen are going to take the high moral position of discharging the Chinese and Japanese because they get a benefit from the government by the imposition of this duty ?
The hon. gentleman
Order.

The hon. gentleman has asked me a question, and surely I may be allowed to say a word in reply. The hon. gentleman asked me if I would guarantee that the lumbermen would do away with Chinese and Japanese labour if the duty was put on. Of course, I cannot guarantee for them.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen laugh, but it is a very foolish laugh. 1 cannot give a guarantee for them, but I can say that I stood up in this House and advocated a Chinese tax of five times the amount the government was willing to put on.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I would be very glad to deal with the position of the hon. gentleman, because he was a member of this government for many years and had an opportunity of putting on a Chinese tax.
We were the first to put the tax on.

In concluding my remarks, I want to say that when it can be demonstrated to me, when subsidies are granted to railway corporations, and high protective duties are placed upon manufacturers, that corresponding protection is given to the industrial labourers, then I am prepared to support the granting of those privileges. But that is not the condition of things that exists to-day. As I said before, the men who seek protection are the last men who want protection to be given to the industrial classes; but they are the very men, as their history shows, to forward petitions and requests to this House and to every other parliament in this country, against any law likely to provide for any restriction or protection on behalf of the labouring man. That is the position I take. The amendment of the hon. leader of the opposition, speaks of protection to labour; and if he is serious, he will seek to bring about corresponding legislation to protect the industrial classes. When you impose a tariff to protect the manufacturer, you want to have some guarantee that the labourer who makes the article protected shall be paid a minimum living wage. Until that is done, you may introduce all the protective tariffs you please, but you will have no assurance that the labourer is going to receive a share of the protection or be benefited by it in any way.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who spoke just before recess, gave us another example of the many different attitudes adopted by gentlemen who support the government of the day on questions which are directly involved in the debate now going on in this House. Starting out as only a free trader could start out, and comparing the condition of affairs in a country which is most decidedly a country of protection, the United States, with the conditions in a country which is recognized as the ideal free trade country, that is, Great Britain, he drew a distinction very strongly in favour of the mechanic or labourer in Great Britain; but then, realizing that he was somewhat of an anachronism in this House, in dealing with the question in that way, he took the precaution to say that he was not a free trader. Then, proceeding along some other
lines which I shall deal with shortly, he wound up with what may possibly be termed the most ultra doctrine of protection which we have yet heard in this House. He said he would support the opposition's policy of protection if we would add to that protection, legislation fixing a minimum wage for the mechanic. Such legislation, it is needless to say, is not within the province of this House, nor has it been undertaken, so far as I am aware, by any legislature which has authority to enact laws relating to such a subject. While he was giving us these different samples of his financial creed, he told us, possibly with a desire to make it clearer to us, that his ideal of a trade policy was the ideal of the present government. It may be that others who are more familiar with the views that have been enunciated in this House in the past can form a clearer opinion than myself as to what is the ideal of the present government; but, speaking as one who has only heard this present budget debate, I must confess that I am still in very great doubt on that point. There was one keynote struck by the hon. member, perhaps inadvertently, which may indicate more clearly than he did in any other words, just what the policy of the present government is. When he rose, he said he had come here to take in all he could; and, if I am not mistaken, the present policy of the Liberal party can only be reconciled with those of past years on the assumption that they were all intended to take in all they could.
It is too late now in this debate to make any attempt to review the various policies which the Liberal party of this country have put forward. They include the different policies which have been put forward in this debate. The hon. member for Russell (Mr. Edwards) declared in most vehement tones that he was a free trader, and as such he supported this government. The hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) said he was a protectionist, and as such he supported this government; and it is a matter of discussion whether the present government, after having come into power, did not, as has been repeatedly said, steal the clothes of their opponents. But I submit that that question is put too broadly. When the Liberal party are accused of having stolen the clothes of their opponents, it has led to some differences of opinion, and it has also led to some criticism of the opposition for making that charge in one breath, and asserting in the next breath that there ought to be more stringent protection in this country. The difficulty, Mr. Speaker, is this, that when the Liberal party stole the clothes of their opponents, they did not steal them all, they only stole, as it were, their upper garments, and the species of protection which they have put in force may be called a kind of kilted protection, that is, a protection which protects part of the Canadian body, and leaves the Tli
other part as minus the ' breeks ' as a Highlander. We have had very good examples of this in the course of the present debate. For example, the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Ross) described in most glowing terms the prosperity of the principal town in his riding, the town of Oshawa, the great advance which had taken place in the industries of that town, and the consequent prosperity of the country around, declaring that this was entirely due to the fiscal policy of the present government; and he also stated, if I am not very much mistaken, that it was the result of the change from the national policy to the present policy. I wonder if the hon. member took the trouble to ascertain the facts before he spoke. Going over the industries of the town of Oshawa, one by one, I find that every industry in that town is a protected industry, not in any technical sense, in which the term may be used in this House, but protected under the national policy.
The various industries similar to those in Oshawa received a certain amount of protection. Under that protection they prospered and grew, setting their roots deep and wide, and when this government came in and changed the tariff in part in 1897. the tariff, so far as it affected the interests of that town, was left severely alone. That is a part of the stolen clothes absolutely appropriated in full by the Liberal party, and the preferential tariff, of which so much has been said, practically in no way affects any one of the industries in Oshawa. It is no wonder then the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Ross) should have dilated as he did on the prosperity of Oshawa. That town is prosperous, and I am glad to know it, and the country in its neighbourhood is prosperous, largely because of the wages paid the artisans.
But, the hon. gentleman must go a little further back to find the cause of that prosperity. So far as it is due to any fiscal policy, it is due to the policy of the Conservative party inaugurated in 1878-9, and not to any change made since. This is a matter of which I have personal knowledge, because in the riding which I have the honour to represent, we also have a prosperous town, and prosperous for exactly the same reason. In the largest town of that riding, there is not a single industry affected by the fiscal policy of this government. The government left every industry in that town undisturbed, and it was most interesting in the last election contest to hear the former member for that riding, largely interested in one of its particular industries, getting up on platform after platform and declaring that in 1897 his party had wiped out the national policy with a stroke of the pen, and then raising his hands in holy horror at the suggestion of one of the members of the Conservative party in Manitoba, that the duty on agricultural implements should

be wiped out. That, however, is simply in line with all that has been said by these lion., gentlemen in connection with the fiscal policy of this administration. To the extent this government has retained protection, the country has prospered, and I challenge any supporter of the government to show that in any case where they have retained the duties on manufactured articles, which were in the tariff prior to 1896, there has not been prosperity. In fact, I go still further, and challenge any one to show any case in which a reduction of the duties has not reduced prosperity. The government removed the duties on some articles to show their affection for free trade. They took the duty off binder twine, for example, and barbed wire, and it is interesting to know that the prices of these articles have increased in larger proportion than the prices of any manufactured articles on which the duty was maintained. The price of binder twine increased very largely because of the trust, and the removal of the duty made the forming of a trust all the easier. The manufacture of barbed wire has been entirely destroyed in the country, but the prices have increased. Every man who buys barbed wire now has to pay a good fair toll to the freight carriers and others who bring it into the country.
The hon. gentleman who spoke just before recess, the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Smith), made some rather vigorous statements about the evils caused by protection, which he described as class legislation, or legislation in favour of the manufacturers. He said, in language that I cannot hope to imitate, that it was an injury to the industrial classes. Why, Sir, the whole foundation of the national policy is the retaining of work in this country for our workingmen. The whole argument, from beginning to end, in favour of the national policy, from the time it was first introduced, was that it would enable us to manufacture in our own country the articles that we use, and thus give employment to our industrial classes. And never before has the contention been so openly made that protection could possibly be an injury to the industrial classes, though it has often been said that protection was class legislation, not so much because it was for the benefit of tbe manufacturers, as because it was for the benefit of those who labour in the factories. This question was treated in that way in the elections that took place a short time ago on the other side of the line. The people of the United States are essentially protectionists, and the free traders, who are making an attack on protection there, have to do it in the veiled way as that which the free traders in this country have to adopt. The question was whether protection should be maintained, and what was taken as the type of protection ? The full dinner pail, nor was the propriety of that being taken as the type for one Mr. LA YELL.
moment questioned. Surely it is too late in the day, with the many years' experience we have had, to intimate for one moment that protection is not a benefit to the industrial classes who work in our shops and factories. The hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Smith) spoke about the men working in the coal' mines, and compared their lot with that of the coal miners of England. But, the members of this House must have noticed that when the hon. gentleman want. ed to .pick out a class in the United States, which may not be benefited by protection, he picked out a- class that is notoriously drawn from the lowest populations of Europe-not skilled labourers, not the men who work in protected factories, hut the men who went into that country from various European countries and worked there in sets and gangs, and even then I question if, looking at the subject from the widest standpoint, his statement would bear examination for a moment. If he had taken as an example the men who work in the factories, if he had taken the men who work in the woollen mills, about which there has been so much discussion, lie would have found a vast difference between their status and the status of the same class of men in a free trade country. And it is because such a difference was noticed years ago by tbe great leader of tbe Conservatives, under whom the national policy was inaugurated, that the national policy was adopted by the Canadian people and put so successfully in force.
The hon. gentleman confined himself to the example of labourers in the mines of the United States, trusting to his sweeping statement, that protection must of necessity injure those who are working in the factories, and who come under the heading of industrial classes. I say that our experience under the present fiscal tariff proves the contrary. The instances I have just mentioned, given us by the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Boss), prove the contrary. In those factories, which have been properly protected, the men are working at good wages, and the towns they inhabit are prosperous. In those where the duties have been reduced, the men are without work, or are working at lower wages, and the towns are not prosperous. I regret to say that in the riding I represent, there is a woollen mill which has been seriously affected from tbe causes mentioned by the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Ken-dry). But. there is another result that I might mention. At the time when this preferential tariff came into force, affecting as it did principally our woollen and cotton mills, tbe farmers of this country found a very large home market for their wool, and' prices ruled from 20 to 25 cents per pound. But gradually, as the preferential tariff went into operation, our woollen mills had to reduce the prices, and to-day our farmers are only getting 15 cents and 10
cents for their wool, as compared with 22 cents and 25 cents. This shows how incidentally protection to one class of men equally protects a large number of other classes.
One interesting result of this debate is that we have had from the leaders of the Liberal party another statement of what their policy is. The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs stated in very vigorous language that this tariff now in force is not a protective, but a revenue tariff, and, so far as there was any protection in it, it was purely incidental. And it has been repeatedly said by hon. gentlemen on the other side, that protection is almost impossible so far as certain classes are concerned. They have mentioned especially, over and over again, that the protection was impossible for this class. Now, if this is a revenue tariff and is not intended to give any protection whatever, it is an interesting question to ask how if comes that duties that were protective prior to 1896 are no longer protective, though they remain exactly the same. The right hon. the premier (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) implied in his speech that this was a revenue tariff, because imports increased under it. It becomes an interesting question to ask whether the tariffs of the United States and Germany are also revenue tariffs and not protective, because in those countries imports have increased. These are questions that I will not attempt to answer, but I would suggest that they possibly show some weakness in the argument of hon. gentlemen opposite. But, if this is in part a revenue tariff, and if any credit is to be obtained for the reduction of duties-and 1 presume that none of all those items that are put on the free list can be included under the head of revenue tariff-we have to deal with the dutiable goods only ; and, as I said, the great bulk of these dutiable goods bear the same duties that they did under the former tariff, save so far as the preferential tariff is concerned and so1 far as these reductions have been made year after year on the imports of Great Britain. Part of the policy as declared, was that there should be no change one way or the other. That must be looked upon as a new policy, because, so far as this tariff differs from the old tariff, it differs from it practically in no other way than by these preferential duties, and these have been changed for several successive years-in tact, I think it was last year that the last change was made. If there is no change^ further to be made, that is something brand new this year. Judging from the words we heard in sonorous tones from the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson), one would suppose that it was reprehensible for a party not to have a new policy every year. He spoke with scorn of a policy which he said was old. If it was more than two
years old, I do not wonder at it coming under his displeasure. It does seem as though in the minds of some men in this country it is impossible to retain the same policy for more than a few years in succession. But we have now a statement which I hope will last a few years, of just exactly what the present tariff policy is. If I might be permitted, I think I would say that when we review the tariff policy of the Liberal party for the last few years, we find that though it has had many forms, though they have placed themselves on many platforms, possibly it is not right for us to say (that they have changed completely. I question if they have changed. I think, as I said, that the hon. member for Vancouver expressed it when he intimated that he would take in what he could while he was here. All these policies, from the time when they advocated commercial union, unrestricted reciprocity, and so on, were undoubtedly policies that the Liberal party took up because they thought they would please the country, feeling that when they came into power the fact that they had made strong protests against protection would not prevent them hanging on to protection if they thought that to do so would help them to remain in office. It was a change of policy, but not of spirit. It suggests the case of the doctor in a country village, who, going into a corner grocery was met with a request from a somewhat loquacious German to be told what this new religion was that they were bringing from China. The doctor wished to know what if was he referred to, whether it was buddhism or theosophy. ' No, not that, doctor,' said the German, and he attempted to give a description of what he meant. The doctor at last understood, and said, ' Oh, you meant the doctrine of transmigration of souls.' * Yes,' was the reply,
' vot vos dot?' The doctor attempted to explain, and at last said, ' Well, it is easier to give you an illustration.' He drew the attention of the German to the fact that death must come to every man, which the German admitted with a regretful sigh.
' Now, Strauss,' said he, * suppose that when you die, your soul, when it left your body, instead of going to some unknown region, went into the body of a little canary hanging in a gilded cage, in a lady's boudoir, and fed from her delicate fingers.' The German thought that would be very nice. ' But, one day the door of your cage is left open ; the cat comes in and kills the canary. Of course, your soul must leave the body of the canary and flies out of the window and takes refuge in a beautiful lily blooming in the garden and shedding its fragrance on the air.' ' Yes,' said the German, ' dot is goot.' ' But, your soul cannot stay in the lily, because a careless servant leaves the gate open, a donkey comes in and bites off your head, and your soul passes into the donkey. You are

driven out of the garden, and as you go out some old friend meets you and looks you in the face and strokes your long ears and says, " Oh, Strauss, mein old friend, how leedle you haf changed." ' Having listened to the speeches here and to the speeches on various platforms in this country, the only conclusion that one can come to is that though the form has changed, there is vefty little change in the true inner soul of the policy held by the Liberal party or their leader. They are prepared for any change, and now they have grown so used to changes that they cannot understand how a party can maintain the same principle for a dozen years. It is a bad condition of affairs in this country when it is possible for a great party not only to change its views when any occasion of party exigencies seems to requre it, but to speak words of scorn against another party which, having tried a great principle and found it to be in the best interests of the country, retains it and backs it up. Seeing the criticism to which the Conservative party is subjected by the hon. gentlemen opposite, this is all the more remarkable inasmuch as, in some lines, hon. gentlemen opposite have really gone further in the line of protection than have the Conservative party when in power, although still maintaining that the fiscal policy is one of a revenue tariff. No attempt has been made to answer the questions thrown across the floor of the House : How can bounties on iron be part of a revenue tariff ? How is the maintenance of duties of 30 and 35 per cent on articles imported into this country, part of a revenue tariff ? How Is even the maintenance of a duty of 27 i per cent on biscuits part of a revenue tariff ? The hon. Minister of Customs referred to that the other day, and, in very vigorous language called attention to the tremendous reduction caused not by his tariff, but by the preferential duties, showing that It was down really to 2oi per cent, only i per cent higher than it was for most of the time when the national policy was in force under the Conservative government. And that reduction was not due to the tariff policy as enunciated in 1897, but was due almost entirely to the preferential tariff. Now, incidentally, before I sit down, I wish to say something about the line that has been taken over and over again by hon. gentlemen opposite, when they said it was simply impossible to give protection to the farming community or to the industrial class. Until the hon. member for Vancouver spoke, I was under the impression that that class meant the industrial class of this country so far as they worked in manufacturing. But the hon. gentleman seemed to confine himself to an attack on capitalists. Now, as to that, it must be recognized by every person in this country that capital and labour are so indissolubly unit-Mr. LAVELL.
ed that they cannot be separated-it is impossible to get a divorce. I would refer the hon. gentleman to his friend the Liberal leader of Ontario, who, when he was asked that in granting certain franchises it should be provided that only home labour should be employed, distinctly refused on the ground that capitalists should be free to select their own labour. That, possibly, is going further than the Conservative party offered to go before. But that is the principle of the leader of the Liberals in the Ontario House.
He said that this was simply legislation for a class ; it has been said over and over again, and I presume the hon, gentleman meant the industrial class. They have insisted that the farmers were not benefited. If the farmers were not benefited, it would be interesting to see some hon. gentlemen opposite analyse the tariff so far as it affects agricultural products. If this is only a revenue tariff and if the farmers cannot be protected, why is there three cents a dozen on eggs ? If it is not there for revenue, and if the farmers cannot be protected, was it put there to blind their eyes ? Was it put there hypocritically ? Was it put there as a species of farce ? If the farmers cannot be protected in any way, why are duties maintained on these agricultural products, when they practically got no revenue, when it means nothing in the way of revenue ? It would be interesting to have an explanation of that. I maintain that the farming community can be protected, they are not protected simply by duties on agricultural implements, but by the growth of our home markets.
Some hon. members on this side of the House have already referred to the fact that it is impossible for a country purely agricultural to prosper and fulfil its destiny, and that manufacturing countries, on the other hand, are always strong and prosperous. When manufacturing and agricultural industries are closely allied a country reaches its highest development. We have had examples of that truth in Canada. In the lean years when industries were stagnant in Canada, our agricultural population prospered so far as good crops could make them prosperous, but they felt the depression as well as others did. But with the improvement in manufactures, under the operation of the national policy, the farmers prospered as did all other classes of the country. When there is a good home market the farmer must feel the advantage exactly the same as any other citizen will feel it. But no country can have a good home market unless it has prosperous manufacturing industries.
Considerable stress has been laid on the prosperity of the last four years. I am glad to know that the country has been prosperous during the last fouy years. I am glad that Canada has been able to share with
tlie rest of the world in the unexampled prosperity that has prevailed everywhere. But when hon. gentlemen opposite get up and tell us that our prosperity is due to their fiscal policy, they aslc us to assume something that is incapable of proof. As well might a man who goes into a wheat field for the first time, shortly before the wheat is ripe, and when he has gathered the harvest, say : Look, at the harvest I have gathered in. You people who have simply sowed the grain have no credit whatever for this glorious harvest. A country's growth is not of a few days or of a few years. A mushroom will spring up in a night, but not so the maple. Canada is not a mushroom country by any means, and no such industrial development as we have enjoyed during the last four years can be produced simply by the stroke of a pen or within a few hours after the passing of a statute in parliament. The fiscal policy was changed by this government in 1897, but the prosperity of this country began prior to 1897. Our prosperity had been preparing for years, owing to the fact that the previous Conservative government had fostered trade, had fostered the industries and commerce of Canada, and when, by the favour of Providence, good times came, Canada was in a position to take advantage of them. Surely it is recognized as a great general principle that there is a time of quiet growth, a time of underground sprouting, so to speak, before anything appears on the surface. We will, perhaps, during the next month, pass through one of the most disagreeable seasons of our climate, one of the months when possibly nature takes on its most forbidding appearance ; but will any person say that we can have the development of vegetation during the summer months without the preparation of these previous disagreeable months ? In the same way the prosperity of the last four years is not due to the almost imperceptible change in the fiscal policy of the country that took place in 1897. As to that particular feature of the tariff on which hon. gentlemen pride themselves most, the preferential feature, I say without hesitation that it has done infinitely more harm than good, in view of the conditions in which this country found itself when it went into force. It has, in fact, only been in force twelve or fifteen months, with any activity. If you deduct this period and look at the country as it was in 1897, such credit as may be due to any one from legislation must be given to the predecessors in office of hon. gentlemen opposite, to the men who for so many years led the fortunes of the Conservative party.
There are a number of other matters on which I intended to speak, but at this hour it is desirable that the speeches should not be long. I will close by emphasizing the point I made, that where there has been prosperity there has been no interfence by
the present government with our fiscal arrangements, and wherever the present government has interfered, it has done so to the absolute loss and injury of Canada.

ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) Hon. gentlemen opposite are much troubled in their minds about the differences of opinion that they say exists on this side of the House. Well, they put me in mind of the sea birds that come close to the shore in the fall and spring of the year, when the weather is calm, they swim backwards and forwards with the greatest ease ; but when the storm begins, then they cluster together. Wait, gentlemen, till the vote is taken, and then vou will see the difference of opinion that exists. Our friends opposite speak much of broken pledges, they are horrified that pledges have been broken before the public of this great Dominion. Well, if a man breaks his pledge to me once I never trust him. You have heard of the Scotch proverb ; Man cheat me once, deil fa him, man cheat me twice, deil fa me. The people of this Dominion have passed their verdict on the action of the government twice, and they have approved of their policy. The majority of the people of this Dominion have shown that they have confidence in the men who occupy the Treasury benches.
Reference has been made to the preparation of the late tariff for protective purposes, and it has been said that a master mind had prepared that tariff. Now, if my memory serves me right, the government of that day had to send to Washington to get a man to prepare that tariff, and when it was prepared it was something that nobody in this Dominion could interpret or understand. It was the American tariff pure and simple, except, of course, as to the figures of the duties. The meaning and principle of the tariff was* exactly the same. Down in Halifax we found the appraisers and importers quarrelling all the time. The importers said they had to hire one of their clerks all the time to do nothing else but to prepare their entries for the customs-house. One part of an article would be so much a square yard, and you had to make a calculation as to how many square yards would be in a piece. Another article you had to put on your scales and weigh it. Then merchants would send to Ottawa samples of the goods on which they paid a certain rate of duty, and there would be a different interpretation made, and a rebate of duty would have to be ordered. I do not know if there are any importers within the sound of my voice in this House, but I am sure that there is not an importer in Canada to-day who desires to go back to the protective tariff of the Conservative government. It was like nothing in heaven above or in the earth beneath, it was confusion from start to finish.
One thing that the present government have done is to simplify the tariff, they have made it plain, it is easily understood.

One of the things that surprises me, and X may say disgusts me, is the way that some members of this House have come here t<? advocate their own personal interests. long will you halt between two opinions ? If protection be his God, then let him worship that, but if revenue tariff be what is right, then let him vote for revenue tariff.

What is your god ?
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) I will go back in sacred history further than did my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean). When the great patriarch Jacob found that he could not get corn in his own country, he sent his sons to Egypt, and he got free corn, and the present government have so changed the tariff that w-e have free corn in Canada to-day, and therefore they follow the old free trade principles that were practiced in those early days.

You are a few thousand years out.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) There are several other things that I hope their supporters will be able to teach them in that line before the present term of parliament will expire. I am glad to see my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) smiling, and I would remind him that he condemned free trade and said that the people of Britain are ashamed of the ghosts of John Stuart Mill, and Cobden and Bright. Well, he will get few to agree with him in that respect. Gentlemen in this House have the habit of speaking of England as if it meant Great Britain, but to my mind it includes Ireland and Scotland as well as England, and when you come to deal with these trade questions on broad lines it is well to bear in mind that it includes the whole empire. I have no objection to Englishmen, but I like Irishmen better, and I like Scotchmen best of all. The hon. gentleman from East York (Mr. Maclean) stated that free trade has been a failure. Let me point out to him that New South Wales is the colony which has adopted the nearest approach to British free trade, and New South Wales has prospered in a greater measure by far than any other of the Australian colonies. The hon. leader of the opposition stated that in the commonwealth of Australia they would likely have a moderate protective policy. I read the speech of Mr. Barton, the new premier of the commonwealth, and lie stated that there were two parties in Australia, one advocating a protective tariff and the other advocating free trade. He mentioned that several of the premiers of the different colonies were in favour of free trade, but that the policy

that would be adopted would be a revenue tariff, and he Indicated that it would take a year or two after the commonwealth was properly established, before they could arrive at what would be a proper revenue tariff. I want to point out the fallacy of thinking that Great Britain will give a preferential market to Canada and to Canada alone. That is out of the question. If anything comes out of that matter it must be by the commonwealth of Australia, and New Zealand, and the other British colonies combining with Canada. When that will be done, and we place ourselves properly before the British government you may get a hearing whatever the result may be ; but it is very doubtful if Great Britain will depart from her present free trade policy.
The great grievance of hon. gentlemen opposite appears to be about the woollen trade of this country. I remember the time when the woollen manufacturers prospered under a 10 per cent tariff. When I first came to this House there was only a 15 per cent tariff, and there were woollen industries in the country prospering at that time. The tariff was increased to 171 per cent under the Mackenzie government, and there was no complaint In those days of the failure of the woollen industry. Perhaps the most outrageous part of the tariff of the late government was that imposed upon woollen goods. In some instances it ranged as high as from 60 per cent to 70 per cent. Under the preferential arrangement made by the present government with Great Britain, there is a protection of from 21 per cent to 23} per cent on woollen goods, and if the woollen mills cannot thrive and prosper under such protection as that, it would be better for the country to let them go down.
I was amused at the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart), speaking of the preferential tariff, he shook his head, and said there is nothing in it-it is not of the slightest importance. But, then he took up his paper again, and said, there are $13,000,000 of woollen goods imported into this country ; and he almost cried at such a calamity. What became of those goods ? Why, the fashionable ladies of Canada used some of them, which they were enabled to get at cheaper rates than before, the working classes used them, the farmers and fishermen used them, and they were of benefit to the country. The great complaint in this country is, that it is too dear a country to live in. The great object is to induce people to come into the country, and we can only do that by making their supplies as cheap as possible. I was amused at hearing the hon. member for Lanark, the other evening, complain of the absence of ministers from their places in the House, instead of being here to listen to his eloquence. He forgot to say that the benches on his own side, including that of his leader, were also vacant ; so that, the inattention paid to him was as much on
his own side of the House as on this side. He made a speech in which, without considering it from an intellectual standpoint, he worked himself up into a high state of excitement, reminding one of a chief who was preparing his tribe for a war dance ; and speaking of the surplus of the hon. Minister of Finance, he declared that there was no surplus, but a deficit of $1,000,000.
